Euro Digital: Europe is preparing money that will work even without the internet

Euro digital has taken a new step forward in Brussels.

The idea is for any citizen to be able to pay with a digital version of the euro, issued by the European Central Bank (ECB), including without an internet connection.

Payments can be made with a phone, card, online, and offline - and rely less on Visa, Mastercard, and private banks.

### What is already raising questions:
- Limits will be set on how much digital euros can be stored.
- Many stores may be required to accept it.
- Banks fear that some of the money will be taken from their accounts.
- Millions of citizens are concerned about privacy of data.

The ECB promises that digital euro will not replace cash, and offline payments will have an increased level of confidentiality (similar to cash).

However, the discussion in Europe has long gone beyond just the technology.

This is a question of power: do we need public digital money or are we opening the door to too much control over how we pay?

📌 Real Yield: How to tell true DeFi returns apart from a ponzi scheme

Key Takeaways
⏺ Many protocols attract users by promising hundreds of percent in annual yields
⏺ Often, this yield is hollow and is sustained solely by printing endless new tokens
⏺ This post breaks down the concept of Real Yield and why it represents the future of sane crypto

1️⃣ The Printing Press — In past cycles, most DeFi projects lured people with 100-500% annual percentage yields (APY). The catch was that you were paid in the project's own native tokens, which crashed due to hyper-inflation.
2️⃣ What is Real Yield — This is a model where a protocol shares its actual business revenue with investors. The platform makes real money from transaction, swap, or borrowing fees and distributes a portion to users.
3️⃣ Payout Currency — With Real Yield, you are not compensated in volatile native rewards. Instead, you receive highly liquid, hard assets, usually stablecoins like USDT/USDC or blue-chip native coins like Ethereum (ETH).
4️⃣ Sustainability — Even though the yields are more modest (typically 5-15% APY), this framework does not rely on a constant influx of new buyers. As long as people use the platform, you get a cut of the action.
5️⃣ Practice — Before locking up your capital for attractive yields, always investigate the Revenue Distribution model and verify exactly where the payout money is generated.

The Bottom Line

If a protocol promises massive returns paid out in its own token, you are just participating in an inflationary race. A healthy DeFi project must generate actual fee revenue and distribute true profits.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Donald Trump reviewed military options for a full-scale war against Iran to “finish the job,” but has decided, for now, not to move forward.

The report says Trump is concerned that renewed military conflict could hurt the chances of a diplomatic resolution and of dismantling Iran’s nuclear program, and that he’s shown willingness to let indirect talks in Qatar run past the August 18 deadline. He is said to be fine with continuing limited strikes on Iranian targets if Tehran violates the current temporary deal - as it already has, repeatedly.

How are those negotiations going?

Not well. It seems JD Vance’s “historic” face-to-face achievement was a one-off. Washington has been quietly downgraded from talking to the Great Satan to negotiating with the Little Satan instead - a senior Qatari official confirmed that U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Qatari officials in Doha, but there are currently no high-level U.S.-Iran meetings scheduled.

Faced with Iran publicly denying that peace talks even exist, Vance is denying reality right back, insisting it’s merely a “Persian negotiating tactic.” He’s not wrong that rejectionism is a tactic - he’s just wrong about what it’s negotiating for. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed the delegation will skip U.S. officials entirely, meeting only the Qataris in Doha to talk about unfreezing Iran’s own assets. The tactic isn’t stalling for a better peace. It’s stalling for a better payment: extract the MoU concessions first, discuss the nuclear file never.

Iranian officials have shown no willingness to meet U.S. nuclear demands, focusing instead on asserting control over the Strait of Hormuz. Iran says it will impose its “sovereignty and new policy” there regardless of whether it reaches an agreement with Oman, calling the strait a purely internal matter. Reports differ on the nature of the proposed transit fees - Iran calls them mandatory, a regional diplomat calls them voluntary, and Oman’s foreign minister rejects fees outright but leaves room for “maritime service” mechanisms such as safety and pollution measures. Regardless of that distinction, Iran seems set on asserting authority over the waterway: it has already indicated that ships paying “security fees” and following IRGC protocols would get priority transit, while others face delays.

Iran will not make a deal the U.S. can accept. That’s the reality. The only question left is how many more “historic” handshakes, Doha detours, and denied peace talks it takes before that reality mugs Vance the way it mugged the godfather of neoconservatism, Irving Kristol, famously defined a conservative as “a liberal who has been mugged by reality.”

(Amit Segal)

Rubio’s Lebanon Deal: Paper Shield, Live Border

Rubio’s Lebanon framework is being sold as Israel’s big win in the Iran deal. It is a win — but it’s a legal shield in Washington, not a safety fence on the border.

The Wall Street Journal sums up Team Trump’s position this way: 
“On this issue, the vice president backs Secretary of State Rubio; no one on Trump’s team wants to force Israel to hand over all of southern Lebanon to an Iran proxy, as Iran demands.” 

That means the U.S. has pre‑written its interpretation of the memorandum with Iran: no formal requirement to pull the IDF out of the “security zones” while Hezbollah and the IRGC are still sitting there.

Strategically, that matters. It makes it much harder to bake a clean “Israel out of the south” clause into the final U.S.–Iran deal and call it implementation of the MoU. 

Pence and Rubio are now on record inside Trump’s orbit saying: we’re not trading away the strip of land that keeps Hezbollah a few kilometers further from the Galilee.

But the margin is razor‑thin. Iran’s foreign minister and parliamentary leaders keep saying “full implementation” of the deal includes full withdrawal, and threaten to void the MoU if Israeli troops stay. 

Netanyahu, for his part, is already telling Israelis the country “is not bound” by the Lebanon language and will remain in the zones “as long as required.” Two sides, one clause, zero shared reality.

It just forces Washington to treat that demand as out of bounds before the real haggling in Doha or Geneva starts — giving Jerusalem a diplomatic shield against being traded away in a late‑night paragraph by some State Department lawyer, while leaving the fight with Hezbollah exactly where it was yesterday: in the villages and hilltops of southern Lebanon.
